title: Rooftop solar and grid instability: Lessons for India from Sri Lanka blackout
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Disaster and disaster management (grid failure) · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources (solar energy)
summary: Sri Lanka's grid collapsed on October 17 after a sudden loss of supply triggered mass disconnection of rooftop solar inverters, a warning for India as it rapidly expands rooftop solar.
evolution: Editorial page: energy security depends on how we electrify.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil goal; storage and grids are the missing link.
Sri Lanka blackout shows rooftop solar can destabilise a grid.
ideas: The cascade: a large coal plant's sudden output drop pulled down grid frequency; rooftop inverters then disconnected together, deepening the supply loss until the whole grid failed.
GS3 · Energy infrastructure / Disaster management
When thousands of rooftop inverters trip together, a local fault can cascade into a national blackout.
Non-dispatchable power is hard to manage: solar and wind depend on the weather and cannot be ramped up or down by grid operators like conventional plants.
GS3 · Energy
The more non-dispatchable power a grid carries, the more flexibility and backup it needs.

The fix exists but is not enforced: ride-through settings keep inverters connected during disturbances, yet under half of Sri Lanka's rooftop capacity adopted them because of old inverters, unupdatable firmware and weak enforcement.
GS3 · Regulation / Infrastructure
Grid safety standards protect only when they are enforced on every inverter, old and new.
India's warning: CERC recorded 68 disturbances in renewable complexes in three and a half years; stricter enforcement helped at utility scale, but distributed rooftop solar is the next challenge.
GS3 · Energy security
India has tamed utility-scale renewable disturbances; rooftop solar is the next frontier of grid risk.
Plan for the worst day: states should test grids on days of lowest demand and highest solar, study how much rooftop solar each feeder can hold, and plan for losing the biggest supply source.
GS3 · Infrastructure planning / Disaster preparedness
Grid planning must test the worst case: low demand, peak solar and the loss of the largest plant.
keywords: Power that operators cannot schedule on demand (solar, wind)
Rising non-dispatchable generation demands storage and flexible backup.
The measure of balance between electricity supply and demand
A sudden fall in frequency is the first warning that supply has dropped below demand.
Inverter setting that keeps solar connected during voltage or frequency dips
Mandating ride-through settings stops rooftop solar from deserting the grid in a crisis.
How much distributed generation a local feeder can safely absorb
Mapping feeder hosting capacity lets rooftop solar grow without overloading the grid.
Small, dispersed power sources such as rooftop solar and batteries
DERs democratise power but must be coordinated to keep the grid stable.
data: 68 disturbances; 1–7 GW losses
Disturbances in India's renewable energy complexes, January 2022–June 2025
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), via IE
GS3 · Energy security
CERC recorded 68 renewable-complex disturbances (2022–25), with generation losses of 1 to 7 GW.
examples: Sri Lanka's October 2026 blackout
Rooftop inverters' mass disconnection deepened a nationwide grid collapse
GS3 · Energy · Disaster management · Essay
Sri Lanka's blackout shows that clean energy without grid safeguards can turn a fault into a national crisis.
Weak enforcement of inverter standards
Under half of rooftop capacity adopted ride-through settings
GS4
GS3 · Regulation · GS4 · Rule of law
Rules on paper but not on rooftops show that enforcement, not drafting, decides safety.
pyqs: Can India meet 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030; shifting subsidies.
Ecological and economic benefits of solar energy generation in India.
Purpose of the Green Grid Initiative launched at COP26.
India's solar potential and regional variations in its development.
Status and targets of renewable energy.

trend.t: Solar questions moved from falling costs (2015) and status and targets (2016) to regional potential (2020), the Green Grid Initiative (2021) and whether India can meet its renewable goals (2022). In 2025 UPSC asked about solar's ecological and economic benefits in GS1.
trend.watch: Solar is asked in both GS1 and GS3, from potential and benefits to targets and grids. The next likely step is integration: storage, grids and stability.

potential: Rapid expansion of rooftop solar is essential for India's energy transition but poses risks to grid stability. Discuss and suggest measures. (15 marks)
Explain the challenge of integrating non-dispatchable renewable energy into the power grid. (10 marks)
What lessons does Sri Lanka's 2026 blackout hold for India's power sector? (10 marks)

practice.q: Rapid expansion of rooftop solar is essential for India's energy transition but poses risks to grid stability. Discuss and suggest measures.

answer.t: On October 17, 2026, Sri Lanka's grid collapsed for over five hours as rooftop solar inverters disconnected en masse; India, rapidly expanding rooftop solar, faces the same test.

pts.t: Generation at the point of use cuts transmission losses.
Homes become 'prosumers', lowering bills.
pts.ex: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana for one crore households.

pts.t: Uses existing rooftops instead of farmland.
Helps meet non-fossil capacity targets.
pts.ex: 500 GW goal for the next decade.

pts.t: Reduces reliance on imported fuels.
Installation and maintenance create skilled work.
Output varies with weather and cannot be scheduled.
Inverters trip together when voltage or frequency dips, deepening a fault.
Thousands of small systems are hard to monitor and control.
Surplus power at midday strains the grid.
Old inverters and firmware that cannot be updated.
pts.ex: Under half of Sri Lanka's rooftop capacity had ride-through settings.

pts.t: Local feeders were designed for one-way power flow.
Enforce grid standards on all inverters, with firmware updates.
Assess how much solar each feeder can take.
Batteries and pumped hydro to balance supply.
pts.ex: Viability gap funding for battery storage.

pts.t: Real-time visibility and control of distributed sources.
Simulate the loss of the largest supply source and low-demand peaks.
CERC and state commissions to monitor distributed disturbances.

answer.t: Rooftop solar can power India's transition only if the grid evolves with it; standards, storage and smart planning will turn a risk into resilience.

title: Smaller cities can lead the way on climate resilience
where: The Ideas Page, page 11 (Vaishnavi T G Shankar, Vasudha Foundation & Sanjay Sridhar)
syllabus: GS1 › Urbanisation, its problems and remedies · GS3 › Climate change; Disaster management; Conservation · GS2 › Local self-government (urban local bodies)
summary: The writers argue that heat and floods in cities stem from the same planning decisions, and that smaller cities, still growing, can build climate resilience into how they expand.
ideas: One root, two hazards: urban heat and flooding are shaped by the same decisions on land, buildings and infrastructure, yet are handled separately; the IPCC's 'climate-resilient development' joins adaptation, emissions cuts and development.
GS3 · Climate change / GS1 · Urbanisation
Heat and floods in Indian cities share a root in land use and building design, so they need one integrated plan.

Frameworks exist, practice lags: India's long-term low-emissions strategy (UNFCCC), the National Mission on Sustainable Habitat, the Urban Flood Risk Management Programme and heat's status as a notified disaster must now enter routine planning and investment.
GS3 · Disaster management / Climate policy
Recognising heat as a notified disaster opens disaster funds for heat resilience; the next step is routine planning.

Smaller cities can shape growth, not retrofit it: much of urban India and its future housing are in cities still expanding, where today's decisions on roads, drainage and buildings can lock in either vulnerability or resilience.
GS1 · Urbanisation
Smaller cities can avoid the costly retrofits of metros by building resilience into how they grow.
Cooling is a planning question: land use, density, expansion and green cover shape cooling demand; building design and efficiency can cut it substantially.
GS3 · Energy / Climate
Urban form, not just temperature, decides how much cooling a city needs.

Coordination and smart money: master plans, roads, utilities and building rules sit in separate departments; climate must enter project appraisal, existing budgets and grants, with CSR and development finance for pilots and local knowledge guiding data.
GS2 · Urban governance
Climate resilience in cities needs inter-departmental coordination more than new funding streams.
keywords: IPCC idea joining adaptation, mitigation and development
Climate-resilient development treats heat, floods and growth as one planning problem.
Cities hotter than surroundings due to built surfaces
Dense, grey urban form intensifies the urban heat island.
Early infrastructure choices fixing long-term outcomes
Roads and drainage built today create climate lock-in for decades.
Building climate into routine plans and budgets
Mainstreaming climate into master plans matters more than standalone projects.
Notifying heat as a disaster lets states use disaster funds for heat action.
data: Possible cut in cooling demand through building design, energy efficiency and thermal comfort practices
India Cooling Action Plan, via IE
GS3 · Energy / Climate
The India Cooling Action Plan estimates better building design and efficiency could cut cooling demand by 20% by 2037-38.
examples: Heat notified as a disaster
Disaster funds can now be used for heat resilience
GS3 · Disaster management · GS2 · Governance innovation
Notifying heat as a disaster shows policy adapting to new climate risks.
Urban Flood Risk Management Programme
Covers 18 cities
GS1 · Urban floods · GS3 · Disaster management
The Urban Flood Risk Management Programme marks a shift from flood relief to flood-risk planning in cities.
pyqs: Flooding of million cities, including smart ones, and remedies.
Urban flooding as a climate-induced disaster and the policy frameworks.
Infrastructure development vs disaster-risk reduction in sensitive areas.

trend.t: Urban questions moved from social problems of urbanisation (2013) and smart cities (2015, 2016, 2025) to urban floods (2016, 2020, GS3 2024) and Tier 2 cities (2022). Climate-linked urban risk is now asked in GS1 and GS3, and the infrastructure–disaster trade-off came in 2026.
trend.watch: Urban flooding has been asked in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Expect heat and smaller cities next: prepare integrated urban climate planning with examples.
focus: Urban floods and heat as linked climate risks
Disaster funds and frameworks for cities

potential: "Smaller cities offer India its best chance to build climate resilience into urbanisation." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why should urban heat and urban flooding be addressed together? Suggest planning measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Why should urban heat and urban flooding be addressed together? Suggest planning measures.

answer.t: Indian cities face heat and floods every season; India has notified heat as a disaster and runs an Urban Flood Risk Management Programme in 18 cities, yet the two are planned separately.

pts.t: Concrete cover, lost wetlands and poor drainage worsen both.
Green cover and water bodies cool cities and absorb rain.
Master plans, roads and building rules shape both risks.
Heat raises cooling demand and power use.
Informal settlements suffer both.
Climate risk in zoning and project appraisal.
Protect lakes, wetlands and tree cover.
Cool roofs and passive design.
pts.ex: India Cooling Action Plan: 20% cut in cooling demand by 2037-38.

pts.t: Development authorities, public works and municipalities plan jointly.
Plan growth before it locks in.

answer.t: One plan for heat and floods, made early in smaller cities, is cheaper and safer than two crises handled late.

title: Misri to visit Nepal tomorrow, set stage for Balen's likely trip to India this month
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Bilateral agreements · GS3 › Infrastructure: energy (hydropower), connectivity; Disaster management
summary: Foreign Secretary Misri visits Nepal to prepare for PM Balen Shah's likely India visit, with connectivity, hydropower, investment and a trade-treaty update on the agenda after months of strain.
ideas: Repairing ties: after Nepal's PM declined to meet India's Ambassador and the Foreign Secretary's May visit was cancelled, visits by Nepal's Finance Minister and a ruling-party leader began a course correction.
GS2 · India–Nepal
India–Nepal ties show how sustained engagement can repair a relationship after political friction.
Disaster diplomacy builds goodwill: after the August 26 flash flood, India sent humanitarian aid, emergency power support and Bailey bridges, and Nepal's PM thanked India.
GS2 · Neighbourhood First / GS3 · Disaster management
India's quick flood relief to Nepal shows humanitarian assistance as a tool of neighbourhood diplomacy.
Connectivity at the core: roads, railways, air routes and power transmission lines top the agenda.
GS2 · Connectivity / GS3 · Infrastructure
Cross-border connectivity turns geography into shared growth between India and Nepal.
Clean energy as a shared asset: Nepal's large hydropower plans, through run-of-river and storage projects, make power trade central to the partnership.
GS3 · Energy / GS2 · Regional cooperation
Hydropower trade can make Nepal a clean-energy partner for India's grid.

Economic partnership beyond aid: Nepal seeks Indian investment, digitalisation, green manufacturing and tourism, and both sides will discuss updating the trade treaty to cover services, investment protection and profit repatriation.
GS2 · Bilateral agreements
Updating the trade treaty would move India–Nepal ties from aid to investment and services.
keywords: Flood relief and connectivity projects put Neighbourhood First into practice in Nepal.
Using relief to build trust between states
India's flood aid to Nepal is disaster diplomacy that rebuilt goodwill.
Generating power from river flow with little storage
Run-of-river and storage projects underpin Nepal's hydropower ambitions.
Cross-border power trade can integrate South Asia's grids.
examples: Bailey bridges for Nepal after the flood
India's quick relief after the August 26 flash flood
GS4
GS2 · Neighbourhood First · GS3 · Disaster management · GS4 · Compassion in IR
India's flood relief to Nepal shows compassion and strategy working together in neighbourhood diplomacy.
India–Nepal course correction
From snubs to high-level visits within months
GS2 · India and its neighbourhood
India–Nepal ties show patient diplomacy outlasting political friction.
pyqs: China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition.
How domestic factors shape foreign policy towards a neighbour.
Project Mausam and India's neighbourhood outreach.

trend.t: Neighbourhood questions moved from domestic factors in foreign policy (Sri Lanka, 2013) and the Maldives (2013, 2024) to Sri Lanka's crisis (2022) and China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition (2026). Hydropower technology came in GS3 (2013).
trend.watch: Small neighbours, with China's role in the background, keep returning. Prepare India's tools: connectivity, energy trade, disaster relief and economic partnership, with Nepal as an example.
focus: Connectivity and energy trade with neighbours

answer.t: Foreign Secretary Misri's Nepal visit, preparing for PM Balen Shah's India trip, puts roads, railways, power lines and hydropower at the centre after months of friction.

pts.t: Power trade and transit create mutual dependence.
Roads and rail serve citizens on both sides.
Nepal's hydropower can feed India's grid.
Connectivity aids disaster relief.
pts.ex: Bailey bridges after the August flood.

pts.t: Leaders' snubs disrupted engagement.
Past delays bred distrust.
Competing infrastructure offers.
Services and investment not covered.
Complete projects on schedule.
Cover services and investment protection.
Regular high-level exchanges.

answer.t: Roads, rails and power lines can outlast governments; delivering them on time is India's best diplomacy in Nepal.

title: Andhra braces for landfall, rescue teams mobilised in Odisha as Murasu approaches
syllabus: GS3 › Disaster and disaster management · GS2 › Federalism: inter-state cooperation · GS1 › Cyclones · GS4 › Empathy and compassion
summary: Days after Cyclone Arnab, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha prepared for Cyclone Murasu; Tamil Nadu sent 500 electricity staff to help Andhra restore power.
evolution: Cyclone Arnab's rains cause landslides in Odisha; 300 villages marooned in Ganjam (page 11).
Andhra braces for a second cyclone, Murasu (page 7).
Murasu nears landfall; Tamil Nadu sends power crews to Andhra.
ideas: Back-to-back cyclones: less than a week after Arnab, a severe cyclonic storm forced a second round of evacuations and school closures in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
GS1 · Cyclones / GS3 · Disaster management
Back-to-back cyclones test whether preparedness can be sustained, not just mounted once.
States help states: at Andhra's request, Tamil Nadu deployed 500 electricity department personnel in 25 teams to restore power.
GS2 · Cooperative federalism
Tamil Nadu's power crews for Andhra show cooperative federalism working horizontally, state to state.
Turning a hazard into a resource: Andhra's CM asked officials to use the heavy rainfall to fill tanks and reservoirs through efficient water management, and to finish restoration within 48 hours.
GS3 · Water management / DM
Linking flood response with reservoir filling turns a disaster into water security.
Impact beyond landfall: though landfall was in Andhra, Odisha's southern districts were put on high alert and evacuations prioritised.
GS3 · Disaster preparedness
Cyclone preparedness must cover neighbouring regions, not just the landfall zone.
keywords: Inter-state help in disasters is horizontal federalism in action.
States lending personnel and equipment in emergencies
Mutual-aid arrangements speed up restoration after disasters.
Time target to restore essential services
A 48-hour restoration target keeps recovery accountable.

title: Chopper operators in Uttarakhand protest mandatory co-pilot rule
where: Nation, page 7 (Vidheesha Kuntamalla); see also Explained, page 11, on recurring helicopter accidents
syllabus: GS2 › Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies (DGCA) · GS3 › Infrastructure: airways; Disaster management
summary: Minor topic: after a helicopter crash near Joshimath killed six, the DGCA made two pilots mandatory on Char Dham flights; 11 operators say the cost makes services unviable.
ideas: Regulator reacts to a crash: two days after a Char Dham helicopter crash killed all six on board, the DGCA made two pilots mandatory on every flight and required control-room clearance before each leg.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies
A regulator's job is to tighten safety norms when risks are exposed, even at a cost to operators.
Safety vs viability: 11 operators told the DGCA that higher crew, accommodation and logistics costs cannot be absorbed or fully passed on, and threatened to suspend charter services.
GS2 · Regulation / GS3 · Air transport
Safety regulation must weigh compliance costs, or services may shrink or shift to riskier informal operators.
Consultation matters: operators asked for a mutually workable solution; rules made after consultation are more likely to be followed.
GS2 · Regulatory governance
Consultative rule-making balances public safety with the viability of regulated businesses.
keywords: Regulators too close to industry, or imposing costs without balance
Good regulation avoids both capture by operators and overreach that kills services.
Tighter rules where risk is highest
Mountain flying in bad weather calls for risk-based regulation, not uniform norms.
examples: DGCA's twin-pilot rule for Char Dham
Mandatory co-pilot and control-room clearance after a fatal crash
GS4
GS2 · Regulatory bodies · GS4 · Public safety vs commercial interest
The DGCA's twin-pilot rule shows a regulator putting passenger safety ahead of operators' margins.
pyqs: Independence and autonomy of regulatory institutions.
potential: Discuss the challenges faced by regulatory bodies in balancing public safety with the commercial viability of regulated services. Illustrate with examples. (10 marks)
